title: What makes a workflow agentic?
notes:
MODE: TEACH

TIME: 0:45

PURPOSE: Build a concept required for the next application.

LAND THIS: An agent combines a model with tools, an action loop, and a stopping condition.

SAY:
- Use the supplier task: inspect a file, calculate, check, then produce an artifact.
- The agent can choose steps within its authority; a person still defines the goal and reviews important outcomes.
- Distinguish a tool-using action loop from ordinary back-and-forth chat.

DO: None.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 5 · WHAT AN AGENT IS
44
THE MECHANICS
An agent = model + tools + instructions, run in a loop
Gather
read files, search, state
Act
one step: edit, run, query
Verify
check result vs goal
Repeat
adjust — or stop
…until the goal is met, a check fails, or a guardrail says “ask the human”
In the vendors’ words
“Systems that independently accomplish tasks on your behalf” (OpenAI) · models that “dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage” (Anthropic) — a chatbot that answers and waits is not an agent.
Tools — the arms
files, shell, browsers, spreadsheets, email, code. The model requests; the harness executes.
MCP — the standard port
“USB-C of AI”: one open protocol to plug tools into any agent. Linux Foundation-governed since Dec 2025; ~half a billion SDK downloads/month.
Memory = files
Context window = short-term memory; notes, logs, and git = long-term. Nothing survives unless written down — Part 1’s HANDOFF move, run by the machine, is compaction.
Guardrails
permissions, sandboxes, approval gates for consequential actions — covered later this part.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT — 1) Say the equation in the title: “an agent is a model, plus tools, plus instructions — run in a loop.” 2) Trace the loop cards with your finger, INCLUDING the return arrow: gather → act → verify → repeat, “…until the goal is met, a check fails, or a guardrail says ask the human.” 3) Right card: the vendors’ own words — land the contrast: “a chatbot that answers and waits is not an agent.” 4) The four blocks below, one line each: tools (the arms), MCP (the standard port), memory = files, guardrails (own slide later this part). 5) Distinguish from scripts: scripts break when reality varies; agents read the result and adjust. 6) Bridge: “what does that change about the PROMPT? Everything — next slide is the heart of the training.”
ACRONYMS — MCP = Model Context Protocol — the open standard for plugging tools into any agent (“USB-C of AI”). SDK = Software Development Kit. USB-C = the universal connector standard (the analogy).
CONTENT — Loop framing is vendor-verbatim (Anthropic Agent SDK: gather context → take action → verify work → repeat). MCP numbers as of Jul 2026 per the MCP project blog.
v1.8: HANDOFF ≡ compaction named on the memory block (external-review adoption): agents summarize their own thread into a note and reload it — the exact move trainees did as Part 1 homework. Say it as a callback; it demystifies “agent memory” in one sentence.
44

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 5 · PICK THE VEHICLE
46
PICK THE VEHICLE
Chat, workflow, or agent — the path decides
CHAT
You are the loop.
Exploring, drafting, judging as you go. You read every answer and steer every turn — Part 3’s craft, live.
WORKFLOW
The loop is frozen.
Known path, few tools, same steps every time — script it (n8n, Zapier, Power Automate). Cheaper, predictable, auditable. No judgment needed mid-run.
AGENT
The loop runs inside.
Unknown path — the next step depends on what it finds. Brief it, with gates where the judgment stays yours. Your control lives in the brief, not the conversation.
Don’t chat with an agent — hand it a work order.
The decision rule: known path + few tools → workflow. Unknown path, real judgment → agent, with gates. Still thinking it through → chat.
The wrong vehicle costs: an agent on a known path pays judgment prices for clerk work; a workflow on an unknown path is a script that breaks on the first surprise.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT — 1) Frame: “before you write any brief, pick the vehicle — three ways to get work out of the same model.” 2) Three cards LEFT TO RIGHT; say each tagline as the summary: you are the loop · the loop is frozen · the loop runs inside. 3) The decision rule, verbatim — it is the slide. 4) The costs card keeps it honest both ways: agents aren’t the upgrade for everything. 5) Point at the courier: the handover moment — an envelope with a seal, a clipboard, a satchel; you don’t chat with an agent, you hand it a work order. 6) Bridge: “so what goes IN the work order? First, where its parts come from — the inheritance map.”
ACRONYMS — n8n / Zapier / Power Automate = workflow-automation tools — fixed pipelines of steps, no model judgment between them.
CONTENT — v1.8 new slide (external-review adoption, Round 9B-ext-3, held for the Part 5 review and built at the owner’s v1.8 update): the chat/workflow/agent triage is standard vendor guidance (Anthropic “Building effective agents”: prefer workflows for known paths; agents where paths are open-ended). One salvage from the same review lives here in notes: when a prompt feeds a PIPELINE (n8n/Zapier/API), the pipeline can enforce output schemas at the SYSTEM level — structured outputs are an API feature, not a chat technique.
ART — the paper-collage courier is an owner-generated illustration (R16).

title: A mission brief for bounded work
notes:
MODE: TEACH

TIME: 1:00

PURPOSE: Translate delegation into a compact, usable mission brief.

LAND THIS: A mission brief defines the goal, work, checks, authority, and completion condition.

SAY:
- Use a short brief that a colleague could execute.
- Make the completion condition observable.
- Point to the detailed reference checklist for uncommon or higher-risk tasks.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Exercise: turn the analysis into a mission brief”.

IF LATE: KEEP

CONNECTING INSIGHT
Role, context, tone, format, source rules, and acceptance checks specify requirements for the response or artifact. Requirement type names what must be specified; requirement quality describes how well it is written. Context also supplies background facts. Specify how consequential facts constrain the work. The selected artifact determines which types matter: calculation rules for a spreadsheet, behavior and state for a dashboard, narrative and editability for a presentation, chronology and evidence for an email brief, or reading level and fidelity for a document. A role title alone does not guarantee expertise.

ANCHOR: Yes. Keep the central concept if surrounding reference orientations are skipped.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 5 · THE MISSION BRIEF
48
TEMPLATE A1
The mission brief: twelve blocks, each preventing a failure
<role>
behaviours, not titles — “never invents numbers” beats “senior analyst”
<mission>
one goal, one audience, one deadline, “done looks like…”
<context>
glossary, quirks, targets — the tribal knowledge it can’t infer
<environment>
where to read, where to write, what’s forbidden. Inputs are read-only
<inputs>
each source: location, format, what one row means, trust level
<plan>
the steps in order · methods allowed · methods needing permission
<checks>
HARD (stop the run) vs SOFT (flag) — written so the agent can evaluate them
<outputs>
exact deliverable names + the three logs: CHANGES · FINDINGS · OPEN_ITEMS
<process>
phases with human gates: definitions → mid-run review → pre-render approval
<rules>
non-negotiables: never invent data, versioned outputs, assumptions logged
<quality_bar>
done as a checklist the agent must satisfy — and you can audit
<reporting>
exact shape of the final message: status, headline, evidence, open items
The operating-manual test — then ship lean: if a colleague couldn’t run the job from this brief without asking a question, the agent will guess — fix the brief, not the run. Design against all twelve; SHIP the four-section PLAN · DO · CHECK · ACT brief from Part 3, one screen long.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT — 1) Do NOT read twelve blocks. Frame: “each block exists because a specific failure taught someone to add it.” 2) Pick THREE and tell their failure stories: <checks> — the run can fail loudly instead of finishing wrong; <process> — gates catch errors at the cheap end; <reporting> — a status you read in 30 seconds. 3) Gesture over the rest: “the annotated template with a fill-in guide is A1 in your library — and every block is in the Taxonomy Reference with its options.” 4) Amber band, slowly — TWO rules that keep A1 honest. The OPERATING-MANUAL TEST (the agentic upgrade of the show-a-colleague rule): if a human couldn’t play the agent from this brief without asking a question, the AI will guess. And DESIGN THICK, SHIP LEAN: A1 is the design canvas — you think against all twelve blocks; what you SHIP is the lean four-section brief (mission+done · sequence · two HARD checks + ask-first · deliverables). 5) Bridge: “here’s A1 running a real job.”
